**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0760), Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections. All the questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sections: SECTION A (1800 - 1922), questions 1 to 4; SECTION B (1922 - 1961), questions 5 to 8; SECTION C (1961 to present), questions 9 to 12.

Points : chaque question imprime « (25 marks) » et le sujet dit « All the questions carry equal marks » ; `points` vaut donc 25 pour chaque question. Aucun écart constaté entre les points imprimés.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde, puis les 12 questions) : filigrane et publicités gcerevision.com sans conséquence sur la lisibilité ; aucune question n'est coupée ni illisible. Page de garde vérifiée : « JUNE 2020 », ADVANCED LEVEL, History, Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, code 0760, trois heures.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire historiographique, sans accès à un manuel pendant la rédaction ; aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée. Les dates et les faits cités sont ceux de l'historiographie courante du Cameroun, mais n'ont pas pu être recoupés avec une source écrite : à relire par un historien avant publication.

Dates citées de mémoire : Biya président en novembre 1982, « libéralisme communautaire » (1987), rétablissement des relations avec Israël (1986), discours de La Baule (1990), dévaluation du franc CFA (janvier 1994), saisine de la CIJ sur Bakassi (1994), arrêt du 10 octobre 2002, accord de Greentree (2006), transfert de Bakassi (2008), point d'achèvement PPTE (2006), entrée au Commonwealth (1995), sommet de l'OUA à Yaoundé (1996), Conseil de sécurité 2002-2003, lutte contre Boko Haram depuis 2014. Le corrigé juge la formule « continuité et changement » exacte, avec la continuité dominante.

questions.enonce_markdown:
"Continuity and change." How apt is this description of Cameroon's foreign policy under President Biya?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Paul Biya became President in November 1982, succeeding Ahmadou Ahidjo, and he has governed ever since. The statement says that Cameroon's foreign policy under him has combined **continuity** (the maintenance of the principles and relationships inherited from Ahidjo) and **change** (adaptations to new circumstances at home and abroad). This essay argues that the description is **apt, with continuity dominant** in principle and in the main alliances, and change appearing mainly in methods, priorities and new relationships.

**1. Continuity**

- **Moderation, non-alignment and good neighbourliness.** Like Ahidjo, Biya has kept to a moderate and pragmatic policy, respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states, peaceful settlement of disputes, and support for African cooperation. Cameroon has avoided radical or ideological positions.
- **Close ties with France and the West.** France has remained the main political, military, economic and financial partner (cooperation agreements, aid, trade, the CFA franc zone, membership of the Francophonie), and Cameroon has kept links with other Western states, the European Union and the international financial institutions.
- **Commitment to international and African organisations.** Cameroon remained a member of the United Nations, the OAU (later the African Union), and regional organisations in Central Africa (such as the CEMAC and ECCAS), and it hosted the OAU summit at Yaounde in 1996. It has served on the UN Security Council from time to time (for example in 2002-2003).
- **Support for African decolonisation and unity.** Biya continued the traditional position of support for the liberation of Africa and for the OAU's principles, including the inviolability of inherited colonial frontiers.
- **Diplomacy centred on the President.** As under Ahidjo, foreign policy is largely determined by the presidency, with a relatively discreet and cautious style.

**2. Change**

- **Style and priorities.** The "New Deal" of 1982 and Biya's emphasis on "rigour and moralisation", and later "communal liberalism" (1987), brought a style that presented itself as more open, and a growing interest in diplomacy for economic recovery.
- **Economic diplomacy because of the crisis.** The economic crisis of the second half of the 1980s and the early 1990s, falling commodity prices and the devaluation of the CFA franc in January 1994, led Cameroon to negotiate with the IMF and the World Bank, accept structural adjustment programmes and seek debt relief, which it obtained under the HIPC initiative (completion point in 2006). Foreign policy was aimed at attracting aid, investment and debt relief.
- **Response to democratisation and external pressure.** The end of the Cold War, the demands of France and other donors for political reform (the speech of La Baule in 1990), and the internal pressure for multi-party politics led to a more open political system in 1990-1992, and made Cameroon more sensitive to the opinion of Western governments and human rights organisations.
- **Diversification of partners.** Besides France, Cameroon has developed relations with China (and with other Asian and Gulf countries) as providers of loans, infrastructure and trade, and has restored relations with Israel (1986), after breaking them in 1973 under Ahidjo. It also joined the **Commonwealth in 1995**, a notable change for a country with Francophone and Anglophone heritage, which was partly a response to Anglophone demands and to improve relations with the English-speaking world.
- **Border disputes and the use of law.** The conflict with Nigeria over the Bakassi peninsula, which had violent incidents in the 1990s, was brought by Cameroon before the International Court of Justice in 1994. The Court's judgment of 10 October 2002 largely supported Cameroon's claim, and in 2006 the Greentree Agreement set out the terms of implementation, with the transfer of authority in Bakassi to Cameroon in 2008. This was a new approach, relying on international law and mediation, instead of force, and has been much praised.
- **Security and regional crises.** Since the 1990s, and especially since 2014, Cameroon has been drawn into the security problems of the region, including instability in neighbouring Central African states and the fight against Boko Haram in the Lake Chad Basin, with cooperation with Nigeria, Chad and Niger in the Multinational Joint Task Force. The Anglophone crisis from 2016 has also had a foreign-policy dimension in relations with the UN, the Commonwealth and Western governments.

**3. Assessment.** The fundamental orientation (moderation, alliance with France and the West, support for African and international organisations) remained, so **continuity** is the main feature. **Change** is significant, however, in economic diplomacy, in the diversification of partners, in the use of international law over Bakassi, and in the response to new security challenges and political pressures. The description "continuity and change" is therefore **apt**, but with the emphasis on continuity of principle and change of method.

**Conclusion.** Cameroon's foreign policy under President Biya has combined continuity in its basic principles and partnerships with change in response to economic crisis, the end of the Cold War, border disputes and new security threats. The phrase is an apt description, though continuity has been the stronger element.
